IVV and VOO each fell about 7% for the week, tracking SPY's slide because all three hold the same index.

The S&P 500 finished Friday at 6,910.39 after a 265.44-point drop. That close put the index below a number most of Wall Street had treated as the floor for 2026.

Spencer Platt / Getty Images

Less than two hours after the bell, Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello posted on X that at 6,910 the index is up less than 1% for the year and sits "below every major Wall Street firm's price target." He added that reaching the average target of 7,600 would take a 10% rally by year-end.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) fell 3.64% in the session. It later traded at $697.40 after hours.

Fear is building too. The CBOE Volatility Index closed Thursday at 28.44, up 52.1% in a week. When the market sits below every target, the targets were likely too generous from the start, and that matters more to your returns than the size of the gap.

A 3.70% Drop Erased Nearly All of 2026's Gains

Friday's 3.70% fall left the index up just 0.95% from its 2025 close of 6,845.50. The index now sits 11.6% below its October record close of 7,818.93. SPY lost 7.55% over the past week and 9.79% over the past month.

These are interesting times, with Congressional upheaval in the United States amid an uncertain economic environment with rising interest rates, elevated inflation, and potentially slowing economic growth.

It is typically not a great combination for most financial sector stocks, as the sector often serves as an economic bellwether and thrives when the economy is strong. The S&P 500 financials sector has returned just 2.7% year-to-date, which is among the worst performers among sectors.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Many financial stocks have tumbled in recent weeks, caught up in the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 sell-off over the past month. Here are two financial stocks that are at or near 52-week lows that are good long-term buys, even amid the lackluster outlook for the sector in 2027.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Nu Holdings

Nu Holdings (NYSE:NU) is the parent company of Nubank, a Brazil-based bank and financial firm. Nu stock is down 28% year-to-date, but most of that has come in the past month, when the stock has plummeted 17% to its current $11.95 per share, which is hovering near a 52-week low.

The reason for the swoon is almost entirely due to the results of the presidential election in October, where the liberal incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat the conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in a surprise victory.

Most Brazilian stocks tanked after the Lula victory, as the challenger was seen as a better option to spur Brazil's economic growth. But Lula has been in office for three terms already, a time when Nu has been growing like a weed, so it seems like more of a knee-jerk reaction than anything to do with Nu's business model or prospects.

For investors, it is a tremendous opportunity to buy the dip on this valuation reset. Nu stock is trading at just 11 times forward earnings and has a minuscule five-year P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio of 0.13, suggesting it is well undervalued relative to its long-term earnings.

While Nu is the largest bank in Brazil, the low-overhead digital bank has expanded into Mexico and Colombia. And in September, it launched in the United States. Its growth has been impressive, as in the most recent quarter, revenue rose 37% year over year to a record $6.3 billion, gross profit jumped 35% to $2.6 billion, and net income climbed 31% to a record $1.1 billion.

State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) closed at $689.81 on Friday, November 20, 2026. That was a 3.64% drop, after the fund fell in each of the six sessions before it.

Drew Angerer / Getty Images News via Getty Images

The S&P 500 fell 3.70%, or 265.44 points, to 6,910.39. It was the index's seventh straight loss, the longest streak since the one that ended February 28, 2020, when the pandemic selloff began. It also closed below 7,000 for the first time since April 14, 2026, at its lowest level since April 13.

The index is now 11.6% below its October 6 record close of 7,818.93. That puts it in a correction, which means a drop of at least 10% from a record. Even so, the index is still up 0.95% for 2026, so nearly a full year of gains disappeared in about six weeks.

Friday Ties the 2020 Streak for the Longest Run Since the Pandemic Selloff

The February 2020 streak also lasted seven sessions, running from February 20 through February 28, 2020, and it took 12.8% off the index. Longer streaks are rarer. There was one of nine sessions that ended November 4, 2016, and one of eight that ended October 10, 2008.

If the index gains on Monday, November 23, the streak ends at seven. A loss would make it eight, the longest since 2016.

title: The S&P 500 Heads Into Thanksgiving Below Its Peak. Here's How the Holiday Week Has Usually Gone Since 1950.
detail:
The S&P 500 Heads Into Thanksgiving Below Its Peak. Here's How the Holiday Week Has Usually Gone Since 1950.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 1:07 PM CST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) finished on Nov. 16 at 7,416.59, around 5% under the all-time closing high of 7,818.93 it set on Oct. 6. The drop sped up in late October, and the index fell over 4% on Nov. 5 alone as tech stocks sold off.

Chipmakers were among the worst hit that day, amid worries that the midterm election results might slow the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The market is closed on Thursday, Nov. 26, for Thanksgiving, and it closes early (at 1 p.m. ET) the next day.

Historically, this has been a better-than-average week to hold stocks. Since 1950, the index has climbed during Thanksgiving week in 53 of 76 years, or about 70% of the time, and the week's average gain has been roughly 0.7%. By comparison, normal weeks across the same stretch rose 56% of the time and gained roughly 0.2% on average.

But the record looks weaker in years like this one. In the 13 years the index entered the week 3% to 10% under a recent record close, it rose in just seven.

Image source: Getty Images.

Two strong sessions

I measured each year from the close on the Friday before Thanksgiving to the close on the Friday after, with the index's daily closes from Yahoo Finance (which count price moves only, not dividends). That normally includes four trading sessions around the holiday.

Notably, the gains haven't been spread evenly among them. Monday and Tuesday combined averaged a gain of only about 0.1% and finished up in 47 of the 76 years. The Wednesday before Thanksgiving, though, climbed in 58 years and averaged a gain of around 0.3%. The Friday after climbed in 54, with an average gain close to that.

So, the two sessions on either side of the holiday make up almost all the week's typical gain.

The range has been wide, too. The best Thanksgiving week came in 2008, in the middle of the financial crisis, when the index jumped about 12% from around half its record. The worst was 2011, with a loss of nearly 5%.

How about years that started below a record?

To match this year's setup, I looked for weeks that began with the index at least 3% but no more than 10% below its record close, with that record set within around four months. Thirteen years qualified, from 1951 to 2025.

The week rose in seven of them, and the average gain was around 0.4%. That's still a little better than a regular week. But it's around half the average for all 76 Thanksgiving weeks, and the hit rate drops from about 70% to about 54%.

title: His $900,000 Index Fund Is Now More Tech-Heavy Than at the 2000 Peak. Selling $300,000 of Gains at 66 to Play It Safe Makes $34,000 of His Social Security Taxable
detail:
His $900,000 Index Fund Is Now More Tech-Heavy Than at the 2000 Peak. Selling $300,000 of Gains at 66 to Play It Safe Makes $34,000 of His Social Security Taxable
Gerelyn Terzo
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 1:34 PM CST 6 min read
^GSPC
Quick Read

Selling $300,000 of gains pushes a retiree's taxable Social Security from $2,500 to the $34,000 maximum, adding roughly $8,000 in federal tax.

Selling $100,000 yearly triggers the maximum Social Security tax hit three separate times, though each year offers fresh 0% capital gains room.

A single large sale also triggers a 3.8% investment surtax and lifts Medicare Part B premiums by about $5,500 two years later.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Picture a hypothetical 66-year-old single retiree with $900,000 in an S&P 500 index fund, about $300,000 of it unrealized gains.

Thinkstock

Social Security pays him $40,000 a year, and he gets about $10,000 in interest. Today gave him reason to lose sleep: the S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction and the Nasdaq erased its 2026 gain, with technology stocks down about 7% in a single session.

His worry about concentration has numbers behind it. TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins says tech now makes up over 40% of the S&P 500, compared with 35% at the 2000 peak, or 46% if you count tech-related companies. Selling the gains and moving into something calmer feels prudent. What catches most people in his spot off guard is that part of the bill comes through his benefits.

How One Stock Sale Makes His Benefits Taxable

The IRS figures how much of your benefit gets taxed by taking half your Social Security and adding nearly all your other income, capital gains included. For a single person, once that total passes $25,000, up to 50% of benefits can be taxed. Past $34,000, up to 85% can be.

If he doesn't sell, his total comes to about $30,000, and only $2,500 of his benefits are taxable. Add the gains and the taxable amount jumps to $34,000, which is the maximum.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Over the past five years, Dell stock has returned 447%. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) has returned 220%. So $10,000 put in Dell five years ago is now worth about $54,700. The same amount in HPE is worth about $32,000. Dell and HP were once two similar hardware companies. What did Dell do differently? Was it one big decision, or many small ones?

Both stocks fell hard on Friday, Nov 20, as AI stocks sold off. Dell lost 11.0% and HPE 10.1%, while the S&P 500 fund (SPY) fell 3.6%. The returns below include that drop.

First, the gap. Dell beat HPE over one, three and five years. But HPE also beat the S&P 500 by a wide margin. The slow one is HP Inc, the PC half of the old HP. Over five years, $10,000 grew to about $10,600 in HP Inc. In the S&P 500 it grew to about $15,800.

Dell stock is up 447% in five years, and HPE 220%. After gains that big, a sharp drop can be hard to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018. It also pays about 3 times the S&P 500's dividend yield. See how it held up.

The Big Decision: Going Private, Then Buying EMC

In 2013 Michael Dell and Silver Lake took Dell private. That means they bought out the public shareholders, so the stock stopped trading. It took Dell out of reach of quarterly pressure over a shrinking PC business. Revenue had fallen from $62.1 billion in fiscal 2012 to $56.9 billion.

In 2016 Michael Dell closed the purchase of EMC, one of the largest tech deals ever. It made Dell a major storage company alongside its servers. Revenue went from $50.9 billion in fiscal 2016 to $78.7 billion two years later. Dell returned to the stock market in 2018. In 2021 it spun off VMware into a separate company. It used a $9.3 billion VMware dividend to pay down debt.

What Did HP Do Instead?

HP went the other way. In fiscal 2006 HP sold $91.7 billion, 1.6 times Dell's $55.8 billion. In 2015 its board split it into HP Inc and HPE. In 2017 HPE shed its services and software arms. Its revenue fell from $50.1 billion to $28.9 billion in a year. In 2025 HPE bought Juniper Networks.

Last fiscal year, Dell's sales of $113.5 billion topped both HP companies combined, at $89.6 billion. One company was rebuilt by its founder. The other was split up by its board.

Many of the world's most valuable companies today are artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. That's for good reason. The global AI opportunity is truly massive, and many AI hyperscalers are already quite profitable. But what will happen to these companies during a market crash?

Only around 10% of the S&P 500's value is tied directly to companies engaged in developing AI software. However, between 40% and 50% of the index's value is indirectly exposed to AI. That includes major GPU producers such as Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), as well as AI-enabled software providers like Palo Alto Networks and ServiceNow.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

In short, if markets fall, there's a very strong chance AI stocks will lead the way. It would be no surprise to see AI stocks struggle in a market downturn. While high growth rates may support premium valuations, companies with high growth rates already priced into shares typically falter as markets rerate risk tolerances. But as a recent report from BlackRock points out:

Demand for AI compute is growing exponentially with no observed slowdown. AI data center capacity is constrained, driving multiyear, prepaid commitments to lock in scarce AI chip and data center supply. The demand curve has no clear cap: Every leap in capability has been creating appetite for more compute.

If market sentiment becomes risk-averse, pressuring AI stock valuations, investors would be wise to peruse the bargain bin for deals. There's one AI stock I'm keeping a very close eye on, as its underlying fundamentals and already cheap valuation should make it a strong buy during a market crash.

This is my favorite AI stock during a market crash

During market crashes or economic downturns, companies with strong fundamentals often have an opportunity to grow stronger. That's because weaker competitors may face financial difficulties and exit the market. Acquisition prices get cheaper, with expansion opportunities facing less competition.

When conducting a meta-analysis of firms entering a downturn with strong financials and end-market demand, McKinsey & Co. found that these businesses "emerged much stronger coming out of the downturn, and the advantage they gained lasted for a long period."

Image source: Nvidia.

With this in mind, it's not hard to see Nvidia as a strong choice -- perhaps the strongest choice -- for investors during a market downturn. There is no denying that Nvidia's core business is exposed to long-term growth tailwinds. Both sales and earnings are currently growing at roughly 100% year over year. Growth rates should reach 50% to 100% annually over the coming years.

Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds.

Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders' cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?
